statement: How many ordered triples $(a, b, c)$, with each of $a, b, c$ in $\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 12\}$, have $a^2 + b^2 + c^2$ divisible by $12$?

choices.misconception: I thought each square had to be divisible by 12 on its own, so I only used the multiples of 6.
I handled the condition modulo 4 correctly but, modulo 3, only allowed all three numbers to be non-multiples of 3, missing the case where all three are multiples of 3.
I saw that all three numbers must be even and stopped there, ignoring the condition modulo 3.
I applied the condition modulo 3, all three multiples of 3 or none, but ignored the condition modulo 4.

hints: Split divisibility by 12 into divisibility by 4 and by 3.
Squares are 0 or 1 modulo 4, and 0 or 1 modulo 3. Work out which combinations of three squares add to a multiple of 4, and which to a multiple of 3.
Modulo 4: all three numbers must be even. Modulo 3: either all three are multiples of 3 or none is. Among the six even numbers, two are multiples of 3.

solutions.reliable: A square is $0$ or $1$ modulo 4, so a sum of three squares is $0 \pmod 4$ only when all three squares are $0 \pmod 4$, that is, all of $a, b, c$ are even. A square is $0$ or $1$ modulo 3, so the sum is $0 \pmod 3$ only when the three squares are all $0$ or all $1$, that is, when $a, b, c$ are all multiples of 3 or none of them is. The even numbers in the set are $2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12$; of these, $6$ and $12$ are multiples of 3 and $2, 4, 8, 10$ are not. So the count is $2^3 + 4^3 = 8 + 64 = 72$. Transferable idea: split a composite modulus into prime-power pieces and use the short list of square residues for each.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
